Backpropagation and Gradient Descent

Where this is used

Every network in this book is trained with the method of this section: the word embeddings of Word Embeddings, the transformer encoders of Transformer Embeddings, the image networks of , and the contrastive models of Multimodal Transformers. Losses and Performance Measures introduces gradient descent and derives the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits; this section continues from there to the gradients of all weights of a network.

The forward pass in From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks left the small network with outputs o1=0.482o_1 = 0.482o1​=0.482 and o2=0.617o_2 = 0.617o2​=0.617 for the targets 1 and 0, a loss of J=0.325J = 0.325J=0.325. Training must change the ten parameters w1,…,w8,b1,b2w_1, \dots, w_8, b_1, b_2w1​,…,w8​,b1​,b2​ so that the loss falls. Gradient descent knows how to do this once it has the gradient, the vector of all ten partial derivatives ∂J/∂w∂ J / ∂ w∂J/∂w. This section shows how to compute it: first by applying the chain rule to the small network, then with backpropagation, which organizes the same computation so that it scales to networks with billions of parameters. It ends with the softmax output and the cross-entropy loss that classification networks use instead of sigmoid outputs and the squared error.

Loss and Gradient Descent¶

For a training example x\mathbf{x}x with targets t\mathbf{t}t and network outputs o\mathbf{o}o, we use the squared error as the loss of one example, with a factor 12\frac{1}{2}21​ that cancels when we differentiate:

J(x;w)=12∑l(tl−ol)2J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l} (t_l - o_l)^2J(x;w)=21​l∑​(tl​−ol​)2
(1)

Here w\mathbf{w}w stands for all weights and biases of the network. The loss over the training set T\mathbb{T}T is the average, J(w)=1∣T∣∑x∈TJ(x;w)J(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{|\mathbb{T}|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{T}} J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w})J(w)=∣T∣1​∑x∈T​J(x;w), which is half the mean squared error of Losses and Performance Measures. For classification, the cross-entropy loss of that section takes the place of the squared error; the method below works for any differentiable loss.

A network is too large and the training set too big to solve ∇J(w)=0\nabla J(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}∇J(w)=0 directly. Gradient descent instead starts with small random weights and repeats the step w←w−η ∇J(w)\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\, \nabla J(\mathbf{w})w←w−η∇J(w) with the learning rate η\etaη, until the loss stops falling or a maximum number of steps is reached. It finds a local minimum, and it can be slow: near a minimum the gradient becomes small, and in long, narrow valleys of the loss the steps zigzag from one side to the other.

Computing the gradient over the whole training set before every step is expensive. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) estimates it from a small random subset, a mini-batch of typically 32 to a few thousand examples. In each epoch, the training set is shuffled and divided into mini-batches, and the weights are updated once per mini-batch. The estimate is noisy, but many cheap steps make more progress than a few exact ones, and the noise helps to leave shallow local minima.

Momentum reduces the zigzag. It keeps a running update Δ\DeltaΔ that accumulates a fraction γ\gammaγ of the previous updates, so that steps in a consistent direction add up while steps that change their direction cancel.

Key Formula: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum
Δ←γ Δ+η∣B∣∑x∈B∇J(x;w),w←w−Δ\Delta \leftarrow \gamma\, \Delta + \frac{\eta}{|\mathbb{B}|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{B}} \nabla J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}), \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \DeltaΔ←γΔ+∣B∣η​x∈B∑​∇J(x;w),w←w−Δ
(2)

For each mini-batch B\mathbb{B}B, the update combines the average gradient of the batch with a fraction γ\gammaγ of the previous update. With γ=0\gamma = 0γ=0, this is plain stochastic gradient descent.

A common schedule starts with γ=0.5\gamma = 0.5γ=0.5 and raises it to 0.9 or higher once training has stabilized (Sutskever et al., see Further Reading). Training Deep Networks describes optimizers that also adapt the learning rate for each parameter. All of them need the same input: the gradient of the loss of one example with respect to every weight.

The Chain Rule on a Graph¶

The loss is a composition of many functions: sums, activation functions, and the squared error. Its derivatives follow from the chain rule. For z=f(y)z = f(y)z=f(y) with y=g(x)y = g(x)y=g(x), the derivative of zzz with respect to xxx is the product of the two local derivatives:

dzdx=dzdy⋅dydx=f′(y)⋅g′(x)\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{dz}{dy} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = f'(y) \cdot g'(x)dxdz​=dydz​⋅dxdy​=f′(y)⋅g′(x)
(3)

Figure 1 draws the composition as a computational graph. The forward pass computes yyy from xxx and zzz from yyy. The backward pass starts at the end with dzdz=1\frac{dz}{dz} = 1dzdz​=1, multiplies by f′(y)f'(y)f′(y) to obtain dzdy\frac{dz}{dy}dydz​, and multiplies by g′(x)g'(x)g′(x) to obtain dzdx\frac{dz}{dx}dxdz​. The backward pass needs the intermediate value yyy from the forward pass, so the forward pass must keep it.

When a value feeds into several functions, its derivative collects the contributions of all paths. For z=f(y,w)z = f(y, w)z=f(y,w) with y=g(x)y = g(x)y=g(x) and w=h(x)w = h(x)w=h(x), the multivariable chain rule gives

dzdx=∂z∂y⋅dydx+∂z∂w⋅dwdx\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{∂ z}{∂ y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{∂ z}{∂ w} \cdot \frac{dw}{dx}dxdz​=∂y∂z​⋅dxdy​+∂w∂z​⋅dxdw​
(4)

In the graph of Figure 2, the backward pass follows both branches back to xxx and adds what arrives. These two rules are all that backpropagation needs: multiply along a path, add where paths meet.

Backpropagation in the Small Network¶

We start with the weight w5w_5w5​, which connects h1h_1h1​ to o1o_1o1​. It affects only o1o_1o1​, so only the first term of the loss depends on it. The chain runs from the loss through o1o_1o1​ and the sum so1=w5h1+w6h2+b2s_{o_1} = w_5 h_1 + w_6 h_2 + b_2so1​​=w5​h1​+w6​h2​+b2​ to w5w_5w5​:

∂J∂w5=∂J∂o1⋅∂o1∂so1⋅∂so1∂w5=(o1−t1)⋅o1(1−o1)⋅h1\frac{∂ J}{∂ w_5} = \frac{∂ J}{∂ o_1} \cdot \frac{∂ o_1}{∂ s_{o_1}} \cdot \frac{∂ s_{o_1}}{∂ w_5} = (o_1 - t_1) \cdot o_1 (1 - o_1) \cdot h_1∂w5​∂J​=∂o1​∂J​⋅∂so1​​∂o1​​⋅∂w5​∂so1​​​=(o1​−t1​)⋅o1​(1−o1​)⋅h1​
(5)

The first factor is the derivative of 12(t1−o1)2\frac{1}{2}(t_1 - o_1)^221​(t1​−o1​)2 with respect to o1o_1o1​. The second is the derivative of the sigmoid, which has the convenient form ϕ′(s)=ϕ(s) (1−ϕ(s))\phi'(s) = \phi(s)\,(1 - \phi(s))ϕ′(s)=ϕ(s)(1−ϕ(s)) and can be computed from the neuron’s output alone. The third is the input that w5w_5w5​ multiplies.

The first two factors are the same for every weight that enters o1o_1o1​. We give their product a name, the delta of the neuron: δo1=∂J/∂so1=(o1−t1) o1(1−o1)\delta_{o_1} = ∂ J / ∂ s_{o_1} = (o_1 - t_1)\, o_1 (1 - o_1)δo1​​=∂J/∂so1​​=(o1​−t1​)o1​(1−o1​). Then ∂J/∂w5=δo1h1∂ J / ∂ w_5 = \delta_{o_1} h_1∂J/∂w5​=δo1​​h1​ and ∂J/∂w6=δo1h2∂ J / ∂ w_6 = \delta_{o_1} h_2∂J/∂w6​=δo1​​h2​, and in the same way ∂J/∂w7=δo2h1∂ J / ∂ w_7 = \delta_{o_2} h_1∂J/∂w7​=δo2​​h1​ and ∂J/∂w8=δo2h2∂ J / ∂ w_8 = \delta_{o_2} h_2∂J/∂w8​=δo2​​h2​. The shared bias b2b_2b2​ enters both outputs, so its derivative collects both paths: ∂J/∂b2=δo1+δo2∂ J / ∂ b_2 = \delta_{o_1} + \delta_{o_2}∂J/∂b2​=δo1​​+δo2​​.

The weight w1w_1w1​ lies one layer deeper. It enters h1h_1h1​, and h1h_1h1​ feeds both outputs, so two paths lead from the loss to w1w_1w1​:

∂J∂w1=(δo1w5+δo2w7)⋅h1(1−h1)⋅x1=δh1x1\frac{∂ J}{∂ w_1} = \bigl(\delta_{o_1} w_5 + \delta_{o_2} w_7\bigr) \cdot h_1 (1 - h_1) \cdot x_1 = \delta_{h_1} x_1∂w1​∂J​=(δo1​​w5​+δo2​​w7​)⋅h1​(1−h1​)⋅x1​=δh1​​x1​
(6)

The bracket collects what flows back to h1h_1h1​ from both outputs, each delta weighted with the weight on its connection. Multiplied with the derivative of h1h_1h1​’s sigmoid, it gives the delta of the hidden neuron, δh1\delta_{h_1}δh1​​. Every hidden delta is computed from the deltas of the layer above, which is why the method runs backward. The pattern is the same for every layer.

Key Formula: Backpropagation
δl=ϕ′(sl) ∂J∂ol    (output layer),δk=ϕ′(sk)∑lwk,l δl    (hidden layers),∂J∂wj,k=aj δk\delta_l = \phi'(s_l)\, \frac{∂ J}{∂ o_l} \;\;\text{(output layer)}, \qquad \delta_k = \phi'(s_k) \sum_{l} w_{k,l}\, \delta_l \;\;\text{(hidden layers)}, \qquad \frac{∂ J}{∂ w_{j,k}} = a_j\, \delta_kδl​=ϕ′(sl​)∂ol​∂J​(output layer),δk​=ϕ′(sk​)l∑​wk,l​δl​(hidden layers),∂wj,k​∂J​=aj​δk​
(7)

The delta of a neuron is the derivative of the loss with respect to its sum. Output deltas come from the loss, hidden deltas from the deltas of the next layer, weighted with the connecting weights. The gradient of a weight is the input it multiplies times the delta of the neuron it feeds.

The gradients of the first layer are much smaller than those of the second: the largest is 0.031, against 0.096 in the output layer. Each step back through a sigmoid multiplies by ϕ′(s)≤14\phi'(s) \le \frac{1}{4}ϕ′(s)≤41​. In a network with many layers this shrinkage compounds, a problem that Training Deep Networks takes up.

The sign of the output delta

The derivative of 12(t−o)2\frac{1}{2}(t - o)^221​(t−o)2 with respect to ooo is o−to - to−t, not t−ot - ot−o. Some texts write the delta with t−ot - ot−o and then add the update instead of subtracting it; both conventions are correct on their own. Mixing them, a delta with t−ot - ot−o and the update w−η∇J\mathbf{w} - \eta \nabla Jw−η∇J, makes the network climb the loss instead of descending it. A numerical check of a few gradients, as in the example above, catches this and most other mistakes in a hand-written backward pass.

The General Algorithm¶

For a network of any size, we number the layers from the input layer L0L_0L0​ to the output layer LNL_NLN​, as in Figure 8. Layer LiL_iLi​ has MiM_iMi​ neurons with the states oi,1,…,oi,Mio_{i,1}, \dots, o_{i,M_i}oi,1​,…,oi,Mi​​, and an extra state oi,0=1o_{i,0} = 1oi,0​=1 carries the bias. The weight wi,k,lw_{i,k,l}wi,k,l​ connects neuron lll of layer Li−1L_{i-1}Li−1​ with neuron kkk of layer LiL_iLi​, so that wi,k,0w_{i,k,0}wi,k,0​ is the bias of neuron kkk. One training step for an example x\mathbf{x}x with target t\mathbf{t}t runs as follows.

  1. Forward pass. Set o0,k=xko_{0,k} = x_ko0,k​=xk​. For each layer i=1,…,Ni = 1, \dots, Ni=1,…,N, compute si,k=∑lwi,k,l oi−1,ls_{i,k} = \sum_{l} w_{i,k,l}\, o_{i-1,l}si,k​=∑l​wi,k,l​oi−1,l​ and oi,k=ϕ(si,k)o_{i,k} = \phi(s_{i,k})oi,k​=ϕ(si,k​) for all neurons, and keep these values. Compute the loss JJJ from oN\mathbf{o}_NoN​ and t\mathbf{t}t.

  2. Output deltas. Compute δN,k=ϕ′(sN,k) ∂J/∂oN,k\delta_{N,k} = \phi'(s_{N,k})\, ∂ J / ∂ o_{N,k}δN,k​=ϕ′(sN,k​)∂J/∂oN,k​; for the sigmoid and the squared error, δN,k=oN,k(1−oN,k)(oN,k−tk)\delta_{N,k} = o_{N,k}(1 - o_{N,k})(o_{N,k} - t_k)δN,k​=oN,k​(1−oN,k​)(oN,k​−tk​).

  3. Backward pass. For each layer i=N−1,…,1i = N - 1, \dots, 1i=N−1,…,1, compute δi,k=ϕ′(si,k)∑lwi+1,l,k δi+1,l\delta_{i,k} = \phi'(s_{i,k}) \sum_{l} w_{i+1,l,k}\, \delta_{i+1,l}δi,k​=ϕ′(si,k​)∑l​wi+1,l,k​δi+1,l​.

  4. Gradients. Compute ∂J/∂wi,k,l=oi−1,l δi,k∂ J / ∂ w_{i,k,l} = o_{i-1,l}\, \delta_{i,k}∂J/∂wi,k,l​=oi−1,l​δi,k​ for all weights.

  5. Update. Change all weights with the optimizer, for example SGD with momentum, after all deltas are computed.

The order of the last steps matters. Step 3 for layer iii uses the weights of layer i+1i + 1i+1, so updating these weights while the backward pass is still running would compute the deltas with wrong weights. Figure 3 shows steps 3 to 5 for one hidden layer.

A bias shared by several neurons, like b1b_1b1​ and b2b_2b2​ in the small network, receives the sum of the deltas of all neurons that use it. Figure 4 shows the graph: the bias fans out to KKK neurons in the forward pass, and their deltas add up on the way back. Convolutional layers in Convolutional Networks use this mechanism on a large scale, since one kernel is shared by every position of an image.

In matrix notation, the backward pass of a fully connected layer is a single product, δi=ϕ′(si)⊙Wi+1⊤δi+1\boldsymbol{\delta}_i = \phi'(\mathbf{s}_i) ⊙ \mathbf{W}_{i+1}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}_{i+1}δi​=ϕ′(si​)⊙Wi+1⊤​δi+1​, where ⊙⊙⊙ multiplies component by component. The backward pass therefore costs about as much as the forward pass, independent of the number of weights: computing each of the millions of partial derivatives separately, as we did for w1w_1w1​ above, would repeat the same products over and over. Deep learning libraries do not ask us to write the backward pass at all. They record the operations of the forward pass as a computational graph and apply the two rules of the chain-rule section automatically, which is called automatic differentiation.

Softmax Outputs for Classification¶

The small network has one sigmoid output per class and the squared error as its loss. Classification networks are usually built differently, and the reason lies in the backward pass. A classifier must finally name one class, a hard assignment that keeps the largest output. Its accuracy changes only when the winning class flips, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere, and gradient descent receives no signal from it (Losses and Performance Measures). Training therefore uses a soft assignment: a probability for each class that changes smoothly with the weights. The hard decision follows at prediction time, by picking the most probable class.

The softmax turns the sums sls_lsl​ of the KKK output neurons, which Softmax calls logits, into such probabilities, and the cross-entropy measures how much probability the correct class receives:

ol=esl∑j=1Kesj,J=−∑l=1Ktllog⁡ol=−log⁡oco_l = \frac{e^{s_l}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{s_j}}, \qquad J = -\sum_{l=1}^{K} t_l \log o_l = -\log o_col​=∑j=1K​esj​esl​​,J=−l=1∑K​tl​logol​=−logoc​
(8)

The exponential makes every output positive, the division makes the outputs sum to 1, and the order of the sums is preserved. Unlike independent sigmoids, the outputs compete: raising one probability lowers the others. With a one-hot target, where tc=1t_c = 1tc​=1 for the correct class ccc and all other targets are 0, the loss is the negative log probability of the correct class. It is 0 when the network gives that class the probability 1, and it grows without bound as the probability approaches 0.

Key Formula: Output Delta for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
δl=∂J∂sl=ol−tl\delta_l = \frac{∂ J}{∂ s_l} = o_l - t_lδl​=∂sl​∂J​=ol​−tl​
(9)

The delta of each output neuron is its predicted probability minus its target. Cross-Entropy derives it; the backward pass then continues exactly as above.

Three properties make this pairing the standard choice for classification.

  • The delta is simple. No derivative of the activation function appears. The delta has the same form as the gradient of a linear output with the squared error and of the logistic regression in Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines: prediction minus target.

  • The delta does not vanish when the network is confidently wrong. With a sigmoid output and the squared error, the factor o(1−o)o(1 - o)o(1−o) multiplies the error. An output of 0.99 for a target of 0 gives the delta 0.99⋅0.99⋅0.01=0.00980.99 \cdot 0.99 \cdot 0.01 = 0.00980.99⋅0.99⋅0.01=0.0098, almost no signal for the worst kind of mistake. With the softmax and the cross-entropy, the delta is 0.99, a hundred times larger.

  • The computation is numerically stable. The exponential overflows for large sums, in single precision above 88.7. Implementations therefore subtract the largest sum from all sums first, which does not change the probabilities, and compute the logarithm directly as log⁡ol=sl−log⁡∑jesj\log o_l = s_l - \log \sum_j e^{s_j}logol​=sl​−log∑j​esj​, without forming tiny probabilities. Libraries combine the softmax and the cross-entropy into one function that receives the sums, not the probabilities, as the warning in Cross-Entropy explains.

Example: The small network with a softmax output

The output sums of the small network are so1=−0.074s_{o_1} = -0.074so1​​=−0.074 and so2=0.478s_{o_2} = 0.478so2​​=0.478. The softmax turns them into o1=0.365o_1 = 0.365o1​=0.365 and o2=0.635o_2 = 0.635o2​=0.635, which sum to 1, unlike the two sigmoid outputs 0.482 and 0.617. Subtracting the larger sum first gives the shifted sums -0.552 and 0 and the same probabilities. For the target t=(1,0)\mathbf{t} = (1, 0)t=(1,0), the cross-entropy is −log⁡0.365=1.007-\log 0.365 = 1.007−log0.365=1.007, and the output deltas are 0.365−1=−0.6350.365 - 1 = -0.6350.365−1=−0.635 and 0.635−0=0.6350.635 - 0 = 0.6350.635−0=0.635. They are about five times larger than the deltas -0.129 and 0.146 of the squared error, mainly because the factor o(1−o)≤14o(1 - o) \le \frac{1}{4}o(1−o)≤41​ is gone.
